papers.title: Potential public health and economic impact of influenza and COVID-19 multicomponent vaccination (mRNA-1083) for adults aged 65 years and older in France
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.25.26368982 v1

summary.one_liner: A static decision-tree economic model estimates the public health and cost impact in France of a combined influenza/COVID-19 mRNA vaccine (mRNA-1083) versus separate high-dose flu and BNT162b2 COVID-19 vaccines in adults aged 65 and older, across five value dimensions.
summary.plain: Flu and COVID-19 both still cause a lot of illness and hospital visits in older adults, and they are usually given as separate shots. This paper is a computer-based estimate of what would happen in France if one combined shot, mRNA-1083, replaced the two separate vaccines for people aged 65 and over. The authors model one typical flu season after the pandemic and add up the expected cases, hospital stays, costs and staff time saved.
summary.why: It is a modelled estimate, not a trial, so the figures depend on the model's assumptions about protection, uptake and strain matching. It is relevant to how countries plan seasonal respiratory vaccination and whether a single injection could raise uptake among older adults.
summary.background:
- Influenza (flu) and SARS-CoV-2 (the COVID-19 virus) are seasonal respiratory infections that are most dangerous for older adults.
- A decision-tree model is a flowchart-style calculation that follows people through possible outcomes (infection, clinic visit, hospital stay) and attaches probabilities and costs to each branch.
- "Static" means the model does not simulate how the epidemic changes over time.
- High-dose inactivated influenza vaccine (HD-IIV) and BNT162b2 are existing comparator vaccines.
- Vaccine coverage rate (VCR) is the share of the target group that gets vaccinated.
- Antigenic drift is gradual change in flu virus surface proteins, which can make the chosen vaccine strain a poor match; egg-adaptation is a change that can occur when flu vaccine viruses are grown in eggs.
- The mRNA platform is the technology behind the vaccine; the text says it allows later strain selection, which may improve matching.
- The headline figures (for example 25,830 cases prevented and EUR69.4 million saved) are model estimates for an average season, and the text does not give their uncertainty ranges in the summary provided.

papers.abstract: Seasonal influenza and SARS-CoV-2 continue to cause substantial disease burden, particularly among older adults. The potential public health and economic impact of introducing combined enhanced influenza/COVID-19 vaccine, mRNA-1083, was assessed, for adults [≥]65 years, versus separate high-dose inactivated influenza vaccine (HD-IIV) and BNT162b2 COVID-19 vaccination. A static decision-tree health economic model for France evaluated five value dimensions with mRNA-1083, in a stepwise approach, during an average post-pandemic season. Health system efficiencies, potential improved protection versus current comparators, avoidance of influenza egg-adaptation effects, and increased vaccine coverage rates (VCR) were assessed in the base case, and a future-looking scenario assessed potential reduced strain mismatch from antigenic drift, due to later influenza strain selection enabled by the mRNA platform. During an average season, mRNA-1083 was estimated to potentially prevent 25,830 medically-attended cases and 4,286 hospitalisations, saving EUR69.4 million in healthcare costs. Replacing separate influenza and COVID-19 vaccinations with mRNA-1083 may generate health system efficiencies, including 439,285 healthcare-provider hours saved. Potential improved clinical protection with mRNA-1083 prevented 2,194 hospitalisations saving EUR11.8 million in treatment costs. Avoiding egg-adaptation effects prevented a further 75 influenza hospitalisations, saving EUR0.3 million. Increased VCR with mRNA-1083 prevented an additional 2,017 hospitalisations, saving EUR10.4 million. Later strain selection could reduce antigenic drift and prevent a further 148 influenza hospitalisations and EUR0.6 million treatment cost on average per season. Results support that mRNA-1083 may improve seasonal respiratory vaccination by combining convenience, health system efficiency and potential for improved protection, higher coverage, and better influenza strain matching in a single injection.

papers.title: Monitoring SNAP and Food Insecurity After the One Big Beautiful Bill Act: Early Evidence from a National Longitudinal Cohort
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.26368514 v1

summary.one_liner: A longitudinal study of 844 low-income U.S. adults tracks SNAP receipt and food insecurity from August 2025 to March 2026, comparing states that did and did not yet enforce the expanded OBBBA work requirement.
summary.plain: In July 2025 the U.S. passed a law (the One Big Beautiful Bill Act) that made it harder to qualify for SNAP, the federal food assistance program, and added work rules. The authors followed the same group of 844 lower-income adults over several months to see whether fewer people got food aid and whether hunger worries changed. They found SNAP use dipped slightly, food insecurity (not having enough food or money for it) rose, and people who left SNAP were about as food insecure as those who stayed.
summary.why: It offers early, individual-level evidence on what happens to people when food aid is cut back, at a time when the government has also reduced its own tracking of food insecurity. Because the study is early and small in scope, its findings should be read as preliminary, and the text does not show how well they generalize to the whole country.
summary.background:
- SNAP (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program): the main U.S. federal food aid program, often called food stamps.
- Work requirement: a condition that adults receive benefits only if they meet work or training hours; the paper concerns an expanded version.
- OBBBA: the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, a July 2025 U.S. federal law that restricted SNAP eligibility.
- Federal poverty guideline: the government's income threshold for poverty; the study focuses on households under 200% of it.
- Food insecurity: a screening-based measure of uncertain or insufficient access to food due to money or resources.
- Longitudinal cohort: the same group of people surveyed repeatedly over time, which lets researchers see changes within individuals.
- Recertification: the periodic process of re-proving eligibility to keep benefits.

papers.abstract: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), signed in July 2025, restricted eligibility for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and expanded its work requirement, while federal tracking of food insecurity was scaled back. Using a national, community-based longitudinal cohort, we examined changes in SNAP receipt and food insecurity between August 2025 and March 2026 among 844 adults with household income below 200% of the federal poverty guideline, comparing participants in states that had and had not begun enforcing the expanded work requirement. SNAP receipt fell from 40.4% to 38.4%, and the share screening positive for food insecurity rose from 48.1% to 51.2%, with no detectable difference by state implementation timing. Adults who discontinued SNAP were as likely to be food insecure (71.1% in March 2026) and as worried about affording food, housing, and utilities as those who continued SNAP, and few had moved above 200% of the poverty guideline. These early findings suggest that need persisted after SNAP ended. As enforcement expands, policy makers should consider measures that keep benefits flowing to eligible people, such as extended certification periods and simplified recertification, and should support longitudinal monitoring of food insecurity. TEASER TEXTFederal changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) in 2025 tightened work requirements just as the government stopped tracking food insecurity. Following the same 844 low-income adults from August 2025 to March 2026, we found that half screened positive for food insecurity and that the share rose over time. People who left SNAP were just as likely to be food insecure, and just as worried about paying for food, housing, and utilities, as those who stayed on, suggesting that need did not end when benefits did.

papers.title: Institutional Distrust as the Most Frequently Reported Barrier to Health Insurance Enrollment in Post-Conflict Liberia: A Mixed-Methods Study Extending the Andersen Behavioral Model with Trust as a Fourth Enabling Resource
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.22.26368698 v1

summary.background:
- Health insurance enrollment: signing up for a scheme that pays part of medical costs.
- Andersen Behavioral Model: a widely used framework saying health service use depends on need, predisposing traits, and enabling resources (money, organization, social support).
- Institutional distrust: doubt that the public body running a scheme will manage funds honestly, deliver promised benefits, or provide good care.
- Mixed-methods: combining numbers from a survey with interviews and group discussions.
- Logistic regression and odds ratios: a way to estimate how much a factor raises or lowers the odds of an outcome, adjusting for other factors. An adjusted odds ratio of 8 means roughly eight times the odds.
- Post-conflict and fragile states: countries recovering from war with weak government institutions.
- Key informant interviews and focus groups: structured conversations with knowledgeable people and small community groups.
summary.one_liner: A concurrent mixed-methods study in four Liberian counties (survey of 542 adults plus key informant interviews and focus groups) finds institutional distrust as the most often named barrier to health insurance enrollment among uninsured adults, and proposes adding trust as a fourth enabling resource to the Andersen Behavioral Model.
summary.plain: This paper looks at why most adults in post-conflict Liberia have not signed up for health insurance, where enrollment is below 15%. The researchers surveyed 542 adults, half insured and half not, and talked with local leaders and community groups to learn why people distrust the scheme. Among uninsured people, distrust of the insurance system was the most common main reason given, though only just ahead of cost and access problems.
summary.why: It argues that trust in institutions should be counted as a core factor in whether people use health services, not just money and distance, which matters for fragile states that run insurance schemes. The finding that trust barely edges out premium cost is a modest difference, and the study's design (one survey, four counties, 16 interviews) limits how far it generalizes; the paper's own reflexivity note also flags possible bias from its authors' experience with a Nigerian insurance program.

papers.abstract: Health insurance enrollment in post-conflict Liberia remains below 15% despite a decade of reform, and the widely used Andersen Behavioral Model gives institutional trust no explicit place among the determinants of service use. We examined institutional distrust as a theoretically distinct barrier to enrollment using a concurrent mixed-methods design in four counties (Montserrado, Margibi, Nimba and Grand Gedeh). A cross-sectional survey of 542 adults (271 insured, 271 uninsured) ranked self-reported primary barriers and modeled enrollment with multivariable logistic regression; 16 key informant interviews and four focus group discussions, one per county, were analyzed thematically, combining deductive orientation to Andersens framework with inductive derivation of trust subtypes, and integrated with survey findings through joint display. Among uninsured respondents, institutional distrust was the most frequently reported primary barrier (57/271, 21.0%), narrowly ahead of premium cost (49, 18.1%) and inaccessibility of services (47, 17.3%), and the barrier distribution did not differ significantly by county. Four analytic subtypes were developed (fund-stewardship, benefit-delivery, provider-quality and generalized-state distrust), although direct evidence for provider-quality distrust overlapped with wider state-health-sector distrust. In multivariable analysis, socioeconomic status was the strongest structural predictor of enrollment: formal employment (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 8.78, 95% CI 4.90 to 15.76), tertiary education (aOR 8.17, 4.12 to 16.20) and secondary education (aOR 7.36, 3.98 to 13.63) each independently raised the odds of enrollment, whereas informal employment (aOR 1.35, 0.81 to 2.24), sex and county were not significant. Socioeconomic status thus structures who enrolls, while institutional distrust is the barrier the uninsured most often name, a pattern the qualitative data corroborate. We propose extending the Andersen model to treat institutional trust as a fourth enabling resource alongside financial, organizational and social-support resources. In fragile states, trust-building should be treated as health-system infrastructure that complements, rather than replaces, financial-access measures. KEY MESSAGESO_LIAbout one in five uninsured adults in four Liberian counties named distrust of the insurance scheme as their main reason for not enrolling, slightly more than named premium cost, and the overall pattern of barriers did not differ significantly between urban, peri-urban, conflict-affected and remote counties. C_LIO_LIDistrust is not a single attitude. Participants distinguished doubts about whether premiums are safeguarded, whether promised services are delivered, whether care under insurance is of acceptable quality, and whether the state acts in good faith; each points to a different policy lever. C_LIO_LIEducation and formal employment remain the strongest predictors of who holds insurance, so trust-building must accompany, not substitute for, measures that lower financial and access barriers for informal-sector households. C_LIO_LIEnrollment strategies in fragile and post-conflict states should budget for trust-building as health-system infrastructure: ring-fenced and audited funds, published benefit guarantees, responsive grievance redress, quality monitoring and inclusive oversight, and studies using the Andersen model should measure institutional trust as an enabling resource. C_LI Reflexivity statementThe author team comprises public health and health systems researchers based at Nigerian institutions and a Liberia-based co-author: the first author is a doctoral researcher at the University of Port Harcourt, one co-author is based at a medical center in Liberia and facilitated field access, and the other co-authors bring experience from a state contributory health insurance program (RIVCHPP) and a university center of excellence in public health research. With most of the team working from Nigerian institutional bases, the team was attentive to the risk of importing assumptions from the Nigerian insurance context. Experience within the team of insurance program administration may have sensitized the analysis to scheme design and stewardship concerns. To examine how these positions shaped interpretation, the lead analyst kept reflexive memos throughout coding, community leaders were consulted on instrument wording, and preliminary findings were presented back to community focus groups in each study county before manuscript preparation. Ethical approvalEthical approval was granted by the Research Ethics Committee of the University of Port Harcourt (December 2024; reference UPH/CEREMAD/REC/MM105/030). A letter of local institutional support for data collection in Liberia was obtained (May 2026). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. Funding, acknowledgements, conflicts of interest and author contributions are given in the Declarations section.

papers.title: Association between Social Media Exposure and Self-Medication Practices: Public Health Implications in Punjab, Pakistan
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.22.26368645 v1

summary.background:
- Self-medication: taking medicines without consulting a doctor or pharmacist about them.
- Cross-sectional survey: a one-time questionnaire that captures a snapshot; it shows associations, not cause and effect.
- Chi-square test: a statistical check of whether two categories (e.g., ad recall and medication frequency) are related more than chance would suggest.
- Multinomial logistic regression: a model that estimates how several factors together relate to one outcome with several categories (here, rarely, frequently, more often).
- p-value: the probability of seeing results at least this strong if there were truly no link; p below 0.05 is the conventional threshold for "statistically significant."
- Nagelkerke R²: a rough measure of how much variation the model explains; 0.205 is modest.
- Sample: 280 adults aged 18–60 who completed a bilingual (Urdu/English) questionnaire, piloted with 30 people first.
summary.one_liner: A cross-sectional survey of 280 adults in Punjab, Pakistan (March–May 2026) describes self-medication frequency and tests associations with social-media use, exposure to medicine advertising, and attitudes, finding only partial and cautiously interpreted links because the overall model was not significant.
summary.plain: This study looks at whether people who see medicine ads and health posts on social media are more likely to take medicines on their own without a doctor. The researchers surveyed 280 adults in Punjab, Pakistan, and found that most reported some self-medication, with fever and stomach medicines the most common. Some links appeared, such as with daily time spent on social media, age, and believing advertised medicines are safe, but the overall statistical model was not significant, so the results are tentative.
summary.why: Self-medication with medicines seen online can carry risks like wrong doses or hidden side effects, and social media is a growing source of health information in many countries. The paper is a small, single-region snapshot, so it cannot show that social media causes self-medication, but it may point to where public health messaging about medicine advertising should focus.

papers.abstract: BackgroundSocial media has become an important source of health information, including information about medicines. Exposure to medicine-related content may affect decisions to use medicines without professional consultation. ObjectiveTo describe self-medication practices and social-media exposure among adults in Punjab, Pakistan, and explore associations between self-medication frequency and demographic, social-media-use, and attitudinal factors. Methods: A cross-sectional analytical survey was conducted among adults aged 18-60 years in Punjab between March and May 2026. The final analytic sample comprised 280 participants. A bilingual (Urdu/English) questionnaire assessed demographics, social-media use and health-content exposure, self-medication in the preceding six months, medicine categories, and attitudes. The questionnaire was reviewed by two clinical experts and piloted among 30 participants. Descriptive analyses, chi-square tests, and multinomial logistic regression were reported using IBM SPSS Statistics; significance was set at =.05. ResultsSelf-medication frequency was reported as Rarely by 117 participants (41.8%), Frequently by 130 (46.4%), and More Often by 33 (11.8%). Fever medicines were reported by 179 participants (63.9%) and gastrointestinal medicines by 96 (34.3%); multiple-response medicine categories were not mutually exclusive. Instagram was the most frequently selected social-media platform. Advertisement recall differed across self-medication frequency groups ({chi}2(22)=35.28, p=.036). Belief that medicines shown in advertisements/posts were safe was associated with self-medication frequency ({chi}2(4)=14.26, p=.007), while perceived risk was not ({chi}2(4)=1.587, p=.811). The multinomial models overall test was not statistically significant ({chi}2(40)=54.07, p=.068; Nagelkerke R2=.205). Likelihood-ratio tests identified associations for daily social-media-use duration ({chi}2(2)=13.085, p=.001), age group ({chi}2(6)=14.930, p=.021), and perceived advertisement safety ({chi}2(4)=10.899, p=.028). ConclusionSelf-medication was commonly reported in this sample. Some social-media-use and advertising-attitude variables were associated with self-medication frequency, but the overall regression model was not statistically significant and the cross-sectional design cannot establish causality. Findings should be interpreted cautiously given the sample composition and reported data limitations.

papers.title: Procedure composition, age and race/color in gender-affirming surgical authorizations of the Brazilian public health system, 2014-2025
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.23.26368723 v1

summary.background:
- SUS (Sistema Único de Saúde): Brazil's publicly funded national health system.
- Hospital admission authorization (AIH): a billing record for a hospital stay or procedure, filed through the Hospital Information System (SIH).
- Procedure codes: standard billing codes for surgeries; the paper uses a version-tracked list to decide whether each code is feminizing or masculinizing.
- Descriptive study: it counts and summarizes what happened, without testing causes.
- Median: the middle value of a set of numbers.
- "Parda": a Brazilian census category for mixed-race people, used in self-reported race/color.
- Composition vs. rate: the shares reported describe the mix of records in each period, not the rate of surgery in the population.
summary.one_liner: A nationwide descriptive study of 1,375 Brazilian Unified Health System (SUS) hospital admission authorizations for gender-affirming surgery from 2014 to 2025, classifying procedures by a versioned code list and reporting procedure mix, age, race/color, and hospital counts.
summary.plain: This paper looks at records of surgeries that Brazil's public health system paid for to help people align their bodies with their gender, from 2014 to 2025. The records are billing forms, so they show which procedures were paid for, not who the patients are or why they had them. The authors found that the share of feminizing surgeries fell over time, and that the two groups of surgeries were made up of very different procedures.
summary.why: Public health records like these are increasingly used to describe gender-affirming care, so the paper's point that billing codes cannot show identity, need, or access is a useful caution for monitoring. The authors say that questions of access and equity would need person-level or patient-reported data, which this design does not have.

papers.abstract: Hospital admission authorizations from publicly financed health systems are increasingly used to describe gender-affirming surgery, although they record billed procedures whose feminizing or masculinizing direction can be inferred from the code, without identifying people, self-reported gender identity or clinical need. This nationwide descriptive study examined the authorizations for gender-affirming surgery processed by the Brazilian Unified Health System from 2014 to 2025, which were selected from 3,888 public monthly state files of the Hospital Information System with a historically versioned classification of procedure codes. Of the 1,375 selected authorizations, 711 corresponded to directly feminizing procedures, 428 to directly masculinizing procedures and 236 to a complementary procedure that was analyzed separately. The feminizing share of the directly classified authorizations decreased from 81.7% (196/240) in 2014-2018 to 72.2% (213/295) in 2019-2023 and to 50.0% (302/604) in 2024-2025, proportions that describe composition within periods of unequal length and cannot be read as population rates. In 2024-2025, bilateral mastectomy accounted for 264 of the 302 masculinizing authorizations (87.4%), whereas bilateral breast reconstruction with silicone implants accounted for 118 of the 302 feminizing authorizations (39.1%). The median recorded age was 35 years in feminizing and 30 years in masculinizing authorizations over the whole period, and 34 and 29 years when the comparison was restricted to 2024-2025. The brown (parda) race/color category was recorded in 42.6% (303/711) of feminizing and 61.0% (261/428) of masculinizing authorizations, in a comparison pooled over the whole period and not adjusted for period or procedure. The number of hospitals habilitated for these surgeries remained at five from 2014 to 2022 and doubled in 2023. All aggregate results were reproduced by an independent pipeline that re-read every original public file. It was observed that the equal numbers of feminizing and masculinizing authorizations in the most recent period resulted from markedly different procedure portfolios, which suggests that the monitoring of publicly funded gender-affirming surgery may benefit from procedure-specific indicators and versioned code definitions, while questions of access and equity would require person-level and patient-reported data.

papers.title: Developing a Stakeholder-Driven One Health Collaboration Framework for Bovine Tuberculosis Control at the Human-Animal Interface in Lundazi and Monze Districts, Zambia
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.23.26368721 v1

summary.background:
- Zoonosis: a disease that passes between animals and people.
- Mycobacterium bovis: the bacterium that causes bovine tuberculosis in cattle; it is related to the human tuberculosis bacterium, which the paper notes district hospitals often cannot tell apart from it.
- One Health: an approach that brings human, animal and environmental health workers together to tackle shared diseases.
- Qualitative study: research based on group discussions and interviews rather than numerical measurement.
- Focus group discussion (FGD) and key informant interview (KII): structured conversations with groups or with selected experts.
- Thematic analysis: a method for finding recurring themes in transcribed conversations.
- Abattoir: a slaughterhouse; carcass condemnation means meat is rejected as unfit.
summary.one_liner: A qualitative study in two Zambian districts (Lundazi and Monze) that used focus groups and key informant interviews to identify barriers to veterinary-medical collaboration on bovine tuberculosis and proposes a five-pillar One Health collaboration framework.
summary.plain: Bovine tuberculosis is a cattle disease that can spread to people through raw milk, undercooked meat, and handling infected carcasses. Researchers held group discussions with 104 people, including farmers, abattoir workers, vets, doctors and officials, in two rural Zambian districts in 2022. They found that human and animal health workers mostly work separately, with little formal coordination, and they proposed a framework for better teamwork.
summary.why: The paper addresses a neglected disease that spreads between animals and people, and it shows how gaps between national policy and district-level practice can leave frontline workers isolated. The authors suggest the framework could also apply to other zoonoses such as brucellosis, anthrax and rabies, but the text does not test this, so that claim remains untested.

papers.abstract: Background: Bovine tuberculosis, caused by Mycobacterium bovis, is a neglected zoonosis at the human-animal interface in Zambia, particularly affecting cattle-dependent rural communities in Eastern and Southern Provinces, where cattle are central to livelihoods, nutrition, and cultural identity. While Zambia has a One Health Strategic Plan 2022-2026 and a One Health Secretariat under Zambia National Public Health Institute, operational collaboration between veterinary and medical sectors at district level remains fragmented, contributing to diagnostic gaps, under-reporting, and continued transmission through consumption of raw milk, undercooked meat, and occupational exposure during slaughter and handling of infected carcasses. The disconnect between national policy and district implementation has created a vacuum where frontline workers operate in isolation despite sharing the same disease burden. Methods: This qualitative exploratory study was conducted in Lundazi District (Eastern Province) and Monze District (Southern Province), Zambia, from February to June 2022. Ten Focus Group Discussions were conducted with 104 participants, including cattle farmers, cattle businessmen, abattoir workers, veterinary and para-veterinary professionals, and medical doctors, and ten Key Informant Interviews were conducted with District Veterinary Officers, District Medical Officers, Ministry of Health officials, and Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock officials. Participants were purposively selected based on their role, experience, and knowledge of bovine tuberculosis and One Health collaboration. Discussions were held in local languages (Tumbuka, Tonga, Chewa), audio-recorded with consent, transcribed verbatim, translated into English, and imported into NVivo 12 (QSR International, Melbourne, Australia) for thematic analysis following Braun and Clarke's six-step approach, with framework matrices for triangulation and trustworthiness. This methodological rigor ensured that diverse voices from community to policy level were systematically captured and compared. Results: Five themes emerged: (1) awareness of bovine tuberculosis, (2) socio-economic impacts, (3) public health impacts, (4) cultural practices and transmission, and (5) collaboration gaps and proposed framework. Medical and veterinary professionals demonstrated excellent awareness, while cattle farmers and abattoir workers showed poor awareness. Socio-economic impacts included reduced milk yield and carcass condemnation. Key barriers to collaboration included lack of diagnostic capacity at district hospitals to differentiate Mycobacterium bovis from Mycobacterium tuberculosis, siloed training curricula, absence of formal round-table coordination mechanisms, and limited funding. An existing enabler was informal collaboration in meat inspection between veterinary assistants and environmental health officers. Based on these findings, a five-pillar One Health Collaboration Framework is proposed. This framework was co-constructed from participant recommendations, making it contextually grounded and acceptable to end-users. Conclusion: Effective control of bovine tuberculosis in Zambia requires institutionalized One Health collaboration, moving from informal ad hoc interactions to formal governance structures. The proposed framework provides a practical, low-cost and contextually grounded roadmap for district-level implementation and is applicable to other zoonoses such as brucellosis, anthrax and rabies. Its implementation can help break the cycle of under-reporting and under-funding that currently sustains zoonotic transmission in rural Zambia

papers.title: Partitioning lifespan inequality in hierarchical study designs with an application to global healthy longevity
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.22.26368689 v1

summary.background:
- Lifespan inequality: how much individuals' ages at death vary around the average.
- Variance: a standard measure of spread; larger variance means more variation.
- Mixture distribution: a population made of subgroups, each with its own rate, combined into one overall distribution.
- Hierarchical design: data nested in layers, such as people within countries within regions.
- Variance partitioning: splitting the total variance into parts attributable to each layer and to chance.
- Global Burden of Disease (GBD): a large international database of health measures.
- Healthy longevity: years lived in good health, as estimated in that database.
- Flat vs. population-weighted mixing: whether each country counts equally or in proportion to its population when combining them.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes a variance-partitioning method for hierarchical study designs, splitting lifespan inequality into between-region, between-country-within-region, and within-country components, and applies it to healthy longevity data for 194 countries from the Global Burden of Disease study.
summary.plain: Some people die at very different ages, and part of that spread comes from differences between groups (such as countries) and part from pure chance among people who face the same risks. This paper offers a way to split the total spread in lifespans into layers: differences between large regions, differences between countries within those regions, and chance variation within each country. The authors apply it to healthy-life data for 194 countries grouped by World Bank income category.
summary.why: It gives researchers a systematic way to say how much of global inequality in healthy longevity lies in regional gaps versus chance, which matters for judging where health policy can reduce differences. The text does not show how the method performs against alternatives, so its practical reach is best treated as a methods contribution pending further use.

papers.abstract: Background: Demographic inequality arises from two sources: heterogeneity among individuals subject to different rates, and stochastic variation among individuals subject to identical rates. Partitioning lifespan inequality into these components has been limited to heterogeneity in single factors or, very recently, factorial study designs with multiple factors. Methods for hierarchical designs have been lacking. Objectives: The goal of this paper is to present a generally applicable method to partition inequality of lifespan (and other demographic outcomes) into components within and between levels in a hierarchical study design. Methods: The analysis treats a heterogeneous population as a mixture distribution. Inequality is measured by the variance and partitioned into components between groups (e.g., geographical or economic regions), between sub-groups within groups (e.g., countries within regions), and stochasticity within sub-groups. The method is applied to global inequality in healthy longevity, using data for 194 countries from the Global Burden of Disease study, divided into four regions according to the World Bank income categories and into countries within each region. Results are compared for flat and population-weighted mixing distributions. Results: The protocol for variance partitioning in hierarchical study designs provides variance among regions, among countries within regions, and within countries. It extends naturally to multiple levels (e.g., states within countries) and to factorial components (e.g., regions defined by combinations of income and education). When applied to global healthy longevity, the dominant source of inequality is stochastic variation within countries, which accounts for 85\%-95\% of the overall inequality. The population-weighted mixing distribution reduces the contribution of between-group variance. Contribution: Some of the largest demographic data sets have a hierarchical organization. The methods presented here make it possible to partition inequality, measured by variance, in such studies.

papers.title: Knowledge of antimicrobial Resistance in Bangladeshi Caregivers of School-going Children: A Cross-sectional study.
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.21.26368630 v1

summary.background:
- Antibiotics kill bacteria but do not work against viruses (such as colds or flu).
- Antimicrobial resistance (AMR): bacteria become able to survive drugs meant to kill them, so infections become harder to treat.
- Self-medication: taking medicine without a doctor's prescription, often on a pharmacist's advice or from an old prescription.
- Cross-sectional study: a one-time survey of a group at a single point in time; it shows associations, not cause and effect.
- Socio-demographic factors: characteristics such as education, location (urban or rural), and household wealth.
- p<0.05: a statistical threshold suggesting a difference is unlikely to be due to chance alone.
- The text gives no details on how caregivers were chosen, the questionnaire itself, or the exact size of the group differences.
summary.one_liner: A cross-sectional survey of 225 Bangladeshi caregivers of school-going children examining their knowledge of antimicrobial resistance, antibiotic use habits, and information sources, with socio-demographic differences in knowledge.
summary.plain: Antibiotics are medicines that fight bacteria, and overusing them lets bacteria evolve so the drugs stop working; this is called antimicrobial resistance (AMR). In this study, researchers asked 225 caregivers of school-age children in Bangladesh what they knew about AMR and how they use antibiotics. They found many gaps: for example, only 35% knew antibiotics do not work against viral infections, and 30% stopped antibiotic courses early.
summary.why: Misuse of antibiotics is one of the main drivers of drug resistance, which makes common infections harder to treat worldwide. The paper gives a snapshot of one group in one country, so it is best read as a local picture that may help shape education and prescribing policy rather than as a general measure of the problem.

papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a critical global health threat exacerbated by inappropriate antibiotic use, yet evidence on caregivers' awareness and practices in Bangladesh remains limited. This cross-sectional study assessed AMR awareness, antibiotic use practices, and information sources among 225 caregivers using a structured questionnaire that also captured socio-demographic characteristics. Understanding of AMR was poor: although 78% recognized that antibiotics are effective against bacterial infections, only 35% acknowledged that they are ineffective against viral infections. Regarding practices, 30% discontinued antibiotic courses prematurely and 40% reported self-medication, primarily guided by pharmacy advice (45%) or previous prescriptions (30%). Healthcare professionals were the leading source of information (55%), followed by media (30%) and community programs (15%). Knowledge differed significantly across socio-demographic groups, with higher awareness among caregivers who were more educated, urban-dwelling, and from wealthier households (p<0.05). These findings reveal a substantial gap between AMR knowledge and antibiotic practices, particularly regarding misuse for viral infections, premature cessation, and self-medication. Targeted educational interventions, stronger enforcement of prescription regulations, and improved healthcare access are urgently needed, and behavioral interventions should address both knowledge deficits and practical barriers to help curb AMR in Bangladesh.

papers.title: Additional Vascular Imaging in Women With Acute Cerebral Ischemia: Thresholds for Cost-Effectiveness
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.26368544 v1

summary.background:
- Acute cerebral ischemia: a stroke where blood flow to part of the brain is cut off, usually by a clot.
- Intracranial vascular imaging: scans (such as CT or MR angiography) that show the blood vessels inside the skull and whether one is blocked.
- M1 occlusion: a blockage in a major artery in the brain (the proximal middle cerebral artery).
- Endovascular thrombectomy (EVT): a catheter procedure that threads into the brain's arteries to physically pull out the clot.
- HERMES: a pooled analysis of randomized trials that measured the benefit of thrombectomy.
- Modified Rankin Scale (mRS): a 0 to 6 scale of how dependent a person is after stroke; scores 0 to 2 are usually treated as functionally independent.
- Decision tree and state-transition model: standard health economic tools that follow patients through possible outcomes and health states over time.
- Cost-effectiveness threshold: the price per quality-adjusted life-year (QALY) a payer is willing to accept; here CAD 50,000 and USD 100,000.
- Sensitivity analysis: rerunning the model with different assumptions to see how robust results are.
summary.one_liner: A decision-tree and lifetime state-transition model estimating how many additional intracranial vascular scans in women with acute cerebral ischemia would need to lead to timely endovascular thrombectomy to be cost-effective under Ontario and US Medicare assumptions.
summary.plain: Women with a sudden stroke caused by a blocked blood vessel in the brain are less likely than men to get a scan that looks at those brain vessels. This paper asks how much extra scanning would need to lead to a clot-removal procedure, and how well that procedure would need to work, before the extra care is worth its cost. The authors used computer models of costs and health over a lifetime, with results reported for Canada (Ontario) and the US Medicare program.
summary.why: The question matters for fairness in stroke care, since a sex gap in access to imaging and treatment is a concrete, actionable problem. The findings are conditional thresholds from modelling rather than measured outcomes, so they indicate what a future prospective program would have to achieve rather than showing that it would pay off.

papers.abstract: Background: Women with acute cerebral ischemia receive intracranial vascular imaging less often than men, but the value of expanding imaging is uncertain. We estimated the treatment rates and functional benefits required for additional imaging to be cost-effective. Methods: We developed a decision tree and state-transition model comparing additional imaging followed by timely endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) for M1 occlusion with current care from Ontario public-payer and US Medicare perspectives. Women-specific 90-day modified Rankin Scale distributions from HERMES were projected over a lifetime. We jointly varied the proportion of additional scans leading to additional timely EVT and the treatment effect relative to HERMES. Cost-effectiveness thresholds were CAD 50,000 and USD 100,000 per quality-adjusted life-year. Program costs represented health-care resources in Ontario and additional payments under Medicare. Results: At variable program costs of CAD 1,000 or USD 1,000 per additional scan, assuming the full HERMES effect and no additional fixed costs or pathway-related harm, expected cost-effectiveness required one additional timely EVT per 48 scans in Ontario and 57 under Medicare (2.07% and 1.74%, respectively). Treatment rates of 3.07% and 2.65% were required for a 90% probability of cost-effectiveness under these assumptions. At three additional thrombectomies per 100 scans and the same costs, treatment effects had to reach 76.9% and 67.3% of the HERMES effect. With the full effect, 1,000 additional scans at this treatment rate yielded approximately 5 additional functionally independent survivors at 90 days. Deterministic analyses restricted to 5 years increased the required treatment rates to 4.44% and 4.22%. Conclusions: Additional vascular imaging in women could be cost-effective when a small proportion of scans leads to timely thrombectomy, provided sufficient functional benefit is retained. Prospective evaluations should assess additional treatment opportunities, functional outcomes and program costs against these conditional thresholds, which depend on projected long-term outcomes.

papers.title: Enhancing Access to and Utilization of Maternal and Child Health Service through Implementation of a District-led Integrated Mobile Health Service Delivery Model in Pastoral Ethiopia: A Multi-Method Implementation Research
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.26368458 v1

summary.background:
- Pastoralists move herds seasonally, so fixed clinics are often far away; the average facility-to-village distance here was 29.6 km.
- MNCH means maternal, newborn and child health; ANC is antenatal care (check-ups during pregnancy).
- Penta-3 is the third dose of a five-in-one childhood vaccine, used as a common coverage marker.
- DHIS2 is a national routine health information database used for facility records.
- Difference-in-differences is a comparison method: it compares the change over time in the intervention areas with the change in comparison areas, to estimate the program's added effect.
- Quasi-experimental means there was an intervention and comparison group but people or areas were not randomly assigned.
- Implementation research studies how a program is delivered in practice, not only whether it works in principle.
- PHC means primary health care.
summary.one_liner: A multi-method implementation study with a non-randomized quasi-experimental (difference-in-differences) design evaluates a district-led, monthly mobile health service model for maternal, newborn and child health in four pastoralist woredas of Ethiopia, using DHIS2 routine data and 143 interviews.
summary.plain: Many people in remote, mobile pastoralist communities in Ethiopia are far from clinics, so they often miss care during pregnancy and for young children. This study tested a monthly mobile health service, run through the local district, that brought antenatal care, vaccines and other services to 20 hard-to-reach villages. The authors report that over one year the service reached about 79,000 people across 190 sessions, and that it was linked to better antenatal and vaccination coverage compared with comparison areas.
summary.why: It addresses a real gap in reaching mobile and remote populations, where standard clinic-based models struggle, and it gives practical lessons on district leadership and community co-design. The design is non-randomized and the outcomes are from routine records, so the effect estimates are best read as suggestive rather than definitive; the text does not show long-term sustainability or costs.

papers.abstract: Introduction: Lack of access to essential health services has remained a significant public health challenge in sub-Saharan Africa. The conventional health service delivery models often fail to account for the mobility patterns and socio-cultural values of these communities. These communities are frequently affected by recurrent droughts, conflicts, floods, and disease outbreaks. This study assessed the contribution of a mobile health services (MHS) delivery model designed to improve access to and utilisation of maternal, neonatal, and child health services in pastoralist contexts of Ethiopia. Methods: A multi-method embedded implementation research with a non-randomized controlled quasi-experimental study design was employed in four selected Woredas of Ethiopia. Baseline data from July 2022 to June 2023 and endline data from July 2023 to June 2024 were extracted from DHIS2. The MHS delivery model was co-designed with stakeholders, redefined communitycentred outreach sites, and established a multidisciplinary team, that was implemented monthly. The average distance between the health facility and the centre of the targeted community village was 29.6 kilometres. Data were captured from routine health service records, MHS databases, and program reports, and 143 in-depth interviews among service providers and beneficiaries. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistical methods and difference-indifferences using Stata 18, while qualitative data were coded and analysed using ATLAS.ti. Results: During the twelve months, the MHS reached 79,404 people through 190 sessions held and offered an integrated essential health service in 20 hard-to-reach villages. In the study area, ANC use was 64.0% in Chifra and 75.6% in Dasenech. In addition, penta-3 antigen vaccination improved from 66.0% to 69.7% in Chifra and from 91.2% to 102.1% in Dasenech, respectively. In the difference-indifferences analysis, the MHS significantly enhanced access to ANC follow-up and completion of pentavalent and full vaccination coverage. A Woreda-led approach, community engagement, context-tailored and timely communication, and comprehensive service delivery by a multidisciplinary team enhanced the use and acceptability of the MHS in the pastoral setting. The contribution of MHS to ensuring access and use of MNCH services ranged from 13.0% to 19.1% for continuing family planning and antenatal care, respectively. Conclusions: The study highlights that the MHS delivery model is a suitable platform that has substantially contributed to improving access to and use of maternal, newborn, and child health services in pastoral, agropastoral, and scattered settlements. Being a woreda-led, participatory codesign, community-centred approach, and context-tailored health service delivery approach enhanced the acceptability and effectiveness of the MHS in reaching the underserved community. Integration of MHS with the existing PHC system, with an innovative, sustainable financing mechanism, is recommended to ensure access and use of MNCH in hard-to-reach settings.

papers.title: Predicting county-level opioid overdose mortality in Ohio through multimodal data: A spatiotemporal study using toxicology and EMS indicators, 2020-2024
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.26368445 v1

summary.background:
- Opioid overdose deaths: the leading cause of overdose death in the US; fentanyl is a major driver.
- Reporting lag: official death certificates and final counts take months to be finalized.
- Urine drug test (UDT) positivity: the share of tested urine samples that show a drug, here fentanyl.
- EMS naloxone events: emergency medical service calls where naloxone, a drug that reverses opioid overdoses, was given.
- Bayesian hierarchical spatiotemporal model: a statistical model that borrows information across neighboring areas (space) and across time periods, and expresses uncertainty as probabilities.
- INLA (Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation): a fast computational method for fitting such Bayesian models.
- Rolling training window: the model is refit using the most recent years of data, moving forward over time, to test predictions.
- Random walk and structured spatial effects: model components that assume each period (or area) is similar to the one before (or next to it).
summary.one_liner: A Bayesian spatiotemporal INLA model for Ohio counties, 2020–2024, that uses urine drug test fentanyl positivity and EMS naloxone events as real-time covariates to predict quarterly opioid overdose deaths, with a two-year training window and random-walk temporal and structured spatial effects.
summary.plain: Official overdose death counts often arrive months after the fact, which makes it hard for health officials to respond in time. This study builds a statistical model for Ohio's counties that uses faster signals, such as drug test results from patients and emergency medical calls where naloxone (an overdose reversal drug) was given, to estimate overdose deaths each quarter. The authors report that adding these faster signals improved predictions, especially during sudden spikes like the early 2020 COVID-19 surge, and that predictions were reliable in large urban counties but weaker in small ones with less data.
summary.why: Reporting lags are a real obstacle to timely response in the overdose crisis, so a method that gives near-real-time estimates could help local planning. The text does not show how well the approach would work in other states or in practice, so its usefulness beyond Ohio remains to be tested.

papers.abstract: Background The opioid crisis is the leading driver of overdose mortality in the United States. While overdose deaths have decreased in recent years, the reporting lag in official overdose deaths presents a hurdle in implementing public health interventions to combat the crisis. Objective To address these data-reporting delays and improve prediction during highly volatile periods, we developed a Bayesian hierarchical spatiotemporal model using real-time drug overdose data sources to predict quarterly overdose deaths across Ohio counties from 2020 to 2024. Methods We implemented a Bayesian spatiotemporal model using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA). Rapid-reporting surveillance metrics, specifically urine drug test (UDT) positivity rates and Emergency Medical Services (EMS) naloxone administration events, were incorporated as fixed covariates. Models were constructed stepwise by first optimizing the spatiotemporal random effect structure and then sequentially adding fixed effects to minimize prediction error. A rolling training window was implemented and evaluated across different training window sizes. Results were assessed overall and stratified by county population size. Results We found that the optimal predictive model structure consists of a two-year training window, a random walk temporal effect, a structured spatial effect, and fentanyl UDT positivity and EMS naloxone events. Incorporating these UDT and EMS data significantly enhanced predictive performance, with the most pronounced accuracy gains occurring during the unprecedented overdose increase associated with the COVID-19 pandemic in the second quarter of 2020. While predictive performance was highly robust in large, urban counties, predictive capability in smaller counties was limited by low data availability. Conclusion Our spatiotemporal prediction model successfully bridges the administrative reporting lags and offers near-real-time quarterly overdose prediction. The study also showed that integration of real-time data sources is especially beneficial for capturing sudden, volatile spikes in overdose deaths.

papers.title: Unmet needs of Polish patients with cystic fibrosis seen through the lens of crowdfunding
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.20.26368008 v1

summary.background:
- Cystic fibrosis (CF): an inherited condition that causes thick mucus in the lungs and digestion, requiring lifelong treatment.
- Medical crowdfunding: people raise money from the public online for health costs, often because public insurance does not pay for them.
- Unmet needs: health-related costs or services that patients must pay for themselves or go without.
- Statistical significance: a rough test of whether a pattern is likely more than chance; "slightly above the threshold" means the evidence is weak.
- Descriptive study: it reports what happened in the data and does not test cause and effect.
- Campaigns come from one website, so the results may not represent all Polish patients or all fundraising.
summary.one_liner: A descriptive analysis of 96 Polish crowdfunding campaigns (out of 2,656 individual medical campaigns, 2009–2017) for people with cystic fibrosis, examining campaign goals, outcomes, and factors associated with reaching the funding target.
summary.plain: People with cystic fibrosis, a inherited lung and digestive disease, in Poland sometimes raise money through public online fundraising pages to pay for things the national health system does not cover. This study looked at 96 such campaigns from a major Polish crowdfunding site between 2009 and 2017. About two-thirds reached their goal, and the funds mostly went to treatment costs, medical equipment, and some non-medical needs such as entertainment.
summary.why: The study suggests that crowdfunding records can show gaps in what public healthcare covers for a specific patient group. The authors report that smaller funding targets were linked to success, while the links for city residence and inhaler purchases were only slightly above the threshold of statistical significance, so these should be treated as tentative.

papers.abstract: Medical crowdfunding allows for funding for needs not covered by the local healthcare system. We aimed to characterize the crowdfunding campaigns for the needs of Polish individuals with cystic fibrosis (CF). In our study, we analyzed data from a leading medical crowdfunding webpage in Poland, focusing on campaigns for individual medical needs initiated between 2009 and 2017. We characterized the features of individuals with CF and the declared goals for which the funds from the online campaigns were intended. Of all 2,656 campaigns, 96 (3.6%) were related to individuals with CF. Approximately two-thirds of these campaigns reached their target amount. Individuals with CF primarily raised funds to cover treatment costs, medical equipment, and entertainment. The successful collection had a significantly lower financial target than unsuccessful campaigns. If the receivers were living in a city or fundraising to gather funds for an inhaler, these were also associated with the campaign's success. However, these associations were slightly above the threshold of statistical significance. Crowdfunding campaigns can be an effective funding source for the needs of patients with CF that are not covered by the public healthcare system. Analyzing crowdfunding efforts for specific patient groups can help reveal their unmet health needs.

papers.title: Does educational attainment change the association between meat intake and obesity? A case-study from urban Brazil.
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.26368245 v1

summary.background:
- Cross-sectional survey: data collected from many households at one point in each year, showing associations rather than cause and effect.
- Body mass index (BMI): a weight-to-height measure used to classify obesity.
- Multivariate estimates: statistical models that adjust for other factors (such as age or income) at the same time.
- Effect modification: when the link between two things (meat intake and obesity) differs depending on a third factor (education).
- Meat substitution: what people eat instead of meat, here sweets and ready-to-eat meals.
- Ultra-processed/ready-to-eat foods: packaged, convenience foods that are often high in fat, sugar, or salt.
- Middle-income country: a nation with moderate average income but large gaps between rich and poor.
summary.one_liner: A cross-sectional study of household surveys from 27 Brazilian state capitals (2018–2023) examining whether education level modifies the association between previous-day meat intake and BMI/obesity, with meat-substitution patterns as a possible explanation.
summary.plain: Brazil eats and produces a lot of meat, and some policymakers want to cut meat production and consumption for climate and health reasons. This study asks whether such cuts would help or hurt health across different groups, using yearly household surveys from Brazil's capital cities. The authors report that among better-educated people, not eating meat the day before was linked to lower body weight and obesity risk, while among less-educated people, eating meat was linked to lower weight gain, with meat more often replaced by sweets and ready-to-eat meals in that group.
summary.why: It bears on whether market or dietary regulation aimed at health and climate has uneven effects across income and education groups. The text is a single observational study, so its associations do not establish that meat causes lower obesity, and the authors' policy conclusion is a suggestion rather than a tested result.

papers.abstract: Brazil is one of the higher meat producer and consumer worldwide. Recently, the sustainability of the meat market is questioned on regard to its high contribution to climate change and public health concerns such as obesity. Hence, further public policies are likely to regulate the meat market and simultaneously reduce meat production and consumption. However, in the context of middle-income countries marked by strong inequalities such as Brazil, the nutritional effect of such market regulation is uncertain. Indeed, one can hypothesize that meat intake plays a protective role against poor nutritious food intake and weight gain among underprivileged settings. To test this hypothesis, this study analyzes household cross-sectional yearly surveys collected from 2018 to 2023 in the 27 Brazilian State capitals. As expected, multivariate estimates show education-specific associations between meat intake and obesity. Among the most educated individuals, declaring not consuming any meat the previous day before the survey is associated with lower body mass index (BMI) and obesity risk, as observed in previous epidemiological studies. By contrast, declaring consuming meat the previous day before the survey appears to be protective against weight gain among poorly educated individuals. We also observe education-specific meat substitution behaviors that help explain these findings. In facts, meat is more likely to be replaced by sweets and ready-to-eat meals among poorly educated individuals compared to more educated ones. We conclude that, everything being equals, meat market regulation policy might worsen public health concerns for under-privileged individuals. Important investments in the education sector and anti-poverty programs are thus needed to limit the raise of nutritional inequalities.

papers.title: Determinants of Tuberculosis Diagnosis Delays among Patients Attending Public Health Facility of Metekel Zone, Northwest Ethiopia, 2024 unmatched Case-Control Study
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.26368197 v1

summary.background:
- Tuberculosis (TB): a bacterial infection, mainly of the lungs, that spreads through coughing and breathing.
- Diagnosis delay: time between first symptoms and the start of proper TB diagnosis; the paper's exact cut-off for "delay" is not stated in the text provided.
- Case-control study: compares people with an outcome (cases, here delayed diagnosis) with people without it (controls) and looks back at what differed between the groups.
- Unmatched: cases and controls were chosen without pairing them on specific traits.
- Logistic regression: a statistical method that estimates how strongly each factor is linked to the outcome; "AOR" (adjusted odds ratio) above 1 means higher odds of delay after accounting for other factors; the 95% CI gives the range of uncertainty.
- Metekel Zone: an administrative area in Northwest Ethiopia.
summary.one_liner: An unmatched case-control study of 210 tuberculosis patients in Metekel Zone, Northwest Ethiopia (2023 data collection), identifying factors associated with delayed TB diagnosis: longer travel distance, rural residence, prior visits to holy water or traditional medicine, and poor TB knowledge.
summary.plain: Tuberculosis (TB) is a lung infection that spreads through the air, and it is harder to control when people are diagnosed late. This study looked at 210 TB patients at public clinics in one zone of Ethiopia to find out what made diagnosis take longer. It found that living in a rural area, travelling more than 10 km to a health facility, going first to holy water or traditional healers, and having poor knowledge about TB were each linked with a longer delay.
summary.why: Diagnosis delay keeps TB spreading and raises the risk of severe illness and death, so knowing which barriers matter can guide local services. The study is a single small local survey, and its findings are associations rather than proof of cause, so they should be read as pointers for local action rather than settled results.

papers.abstract: Background: Tuberculosis Diagnosis delays among tuberculosis patients can worsen infection transmission, disease severity, and mortality risk. Identifying factors influencing delays is crucial due to its persistence across healthcare levels and communities. The study identify determinants of tuberculosis diagnosis delay among patients attending public health facility of Metekel zone, Northwest Ethiopia:2023 Methods: An unmatched case-control study was conducted in Metekel zone health facilities from March to April 2023, involving 210 tuberculosis patients (103 cases, 107 controls) selected through systematic sampling. Data collected through structured questionnaires and STATA used for analysis, including bi-variable and multi-variable logistic regressions. Variables with p-value < 0.25 in bi-variable analysis were included in the final model after checking model fitness and multicollinearity. Results: Overall, 210 tuberculosis patients were included in the study. The following independent variables were associated diagnosis delay of tuberculosis: TB patients who travel greater than 10km (AOR: 2.941, (95 % CI: 1.509, 5.731); TB patients who are living at rural area (AOR: 4.135, 95 % CI :1.759, 9.723); TB patients who prior visit in holly-water and traditional medicine [AOR: 2.978, (95% CI: 1.292, 6.863); poor knowledge about TB [AOR: 2.826, (95% CI: 1.404, 5.687)]. Conclusion: Tuberculosis diagnosis delay is a major challenge to eliminate tuberculosis by breaking the chain of transmission. This study can be attributed to factors including place of residence being rural, poor knowledge about tuberculosis, non-health facility initial actions upon symptom onset, and far distance to health institutions. Recognizing these determinants helps in identifying and addressing barriers inhibiting early diagnosis, potentially improving healthcare access and promoting more timely diagnosis and treatment for tuberculosis patients.

papers.title: Public Acceptability of Self-Payment for Community Pharmacists' Services: A National Online Survey
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.15.26368139 v1

summary.background:
- Community pharmacy: a retail drugstore where pharmacists dispense medicines and provide health services.
- Fee-for-service: a model where each service is paid for separately, rather than through product sales.
- Out-of-pocket payment: money a patient pays directly, not through insurance.
- Non-probability sampling: participants are recruited, not randomly selected from the whole population, so results may not represent all U.S. adults exactly. The sample was quota-matched to population characteristics.
- Between-subjects randomized framing: different groups of respondents saw different versions of the fee question, so their answers can be compared fairly.
- Stated-price vs. any-payment condition: one group was told a specific $20 fee; the other was asked about paying "any amount."
- Trust constructs: survey measures of how much respondents trust pharmacists.
summary.one_liner: A 2026 non-probability online survey of 1,069 U.S. adults tests whether the public would accept out-of-pocket fees for 27 community pharmacist services, with a randomized comparison of a stated $20 price versus an unspecified "any amount" fee.
summary.plain: U.S. community pharmacies have traditionally earned most of their income from selling products, and many pharmacist services are free to patients. This study asked over a thousand American adults whether they would find it acceptable to pay out of pocket for various pharmacist services. Acceptance was higher for some services, such as osteoporosis screening, and much lower for others, such as antibiotic-use consultations.
summary.why: Pharmacies face thin profit margins, so whether patients will pay for services is a practical question for how these businesses might stay open. The findings are based on a non-probability online sample, so they show stated attitudes in one survey rather than measured willingness to pay in real life.

papers.abstract: BackgroundThe traditional business model for sustaining United States (U.S.) community pharmacies has relied on income generated by product sales. A fee-for-service model could help alleviate insufficient profit by monetizing conventionally free pharmacy services if patients are willing to pay out-of-pocket. ObjectivesThis study evaluated public acceptability of out-of-pocket payment for community pharmacist-provided services, variation in payment acceptability across services, and assessed whether payment acceptability differed by respondent characteristics and trust constructs. MethodsThis study represents a cross-sectional online survey of U.S. adults conducted during spring 2026 using a non-probability sampling approach. Primary outcomes were binary stated payment-acceptability judgments for a variety of pharmacist and health services. The survey used a between-subjects randomized payment-framing design, where participants were assigned to either a stated-price condition or an any-payment condition. Secondary outcomes included trust designations and participant demographic characteristics. ResultsA total of 1069 respondents completed the survey. A $20 fee was viewed more favorably than a general "any amount of money" fee. In the $20 stated-price condition, agreement was highest for osteoporosis screening (75.8%) and travel-related vaccines (69.0%), and lowest for antibiotic use consultation (23.9%) and wound care (32.1%). Older respondents and Hispanic respondents were less likely to view payment as acceptable, whereas men and respondents with greater pharmacist trust were more likely to view payment as acceptable. ConclusionAlthough patients historically have received many community pharmacy services at no cost, this study demonstrates that the concept of self-payment ifor certain services is considered acceptable, especially for services not typically provided. Key pointsO_LIIn a quota-matched survey of 1,069 U.S. adults, this study evaluated public acceptability of direct out-of-pocket payment for 27 community pharmacist-provided clinical services. C_LIO_LIPublic acceptability of a $20 out-of-pocket payment varied substantially by service, ranging from 23.9% for antibiotic-use consultation to 75.8% for osteoporosis screening. Higher acceptability was observed for discrete or specialized services, including travel-related vaccines and pharmacogenomic result review. C_LIO_LIPayment acceptability was associated with respondent characteristics and trust in pharmacists. Older respondents and Hispanic respondents were less likely to view payment as acceptable, whereas men and respondents with greater pharmacist trust were more likely to view payment as acceptable. C_LI

papers.title: Determinants of prices of commercial electric breast pumps sold in Germany: a cross-sectional analysis
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.26367926 v1

summary.background:
- Breast pumps: devices that extract milk from the breast; electric ones run on power from mains or batteries.
- Statutory health insurance: Germany's public insurance; it covers pumps only with a medical indication and prescription.
- Flange: the funnel-shaped part that fits over the nipple and areola; sizes vary, and a poor fit can reduce comfort and milk output.
- Cross-sectional study: a snapshot of many items at one point in time, which can show associations but not cause and effect.
- Interquartile range (IQR): the spread of the middle half of prices; the median is the middle value.
- Health technology assessment: a systematic review of whether a medical device is safe, effective and worth paying for.
summary.one_liner: A cross-sectional survey of 282 commercial electric breast pump models from 108 brands sold on German online marketplaces (March 2025 to May 2026) that examines which pump features are associated with higher prices.
summary.plain: Breast pumps are covered by German health insurance only when a doctor prescribes one for a medical reason, so many parents returning to work must buy one themselves. The authors looked at pumps sold on major German online shopping sites and recorded their prices and features. They found a wide price range, from about 20 to about 660 euros, with a median near 73 euros.
summary.why: Out-of-pocket costs for breast pumps may be a barrier to continuing breastfeeding, which links to health equity and consumer safety. The paper is a descriptive price survey, so it shows associations rather than causes, and its findings are most relevant to German policy on reimbursement.

papers.abstract: In Germany, statutory health insurance covers the rental or purchase of breast pumps when a medical indication is present for the mother or infant, and a physician has issued a prescription. However, parents must pay out of pocket for commercially available breast pumps for returning to work or personal circumstances. High indirect costs for continuation of breastfeeding and direct costs for breast pumps and related equipment may pose substantial barriers to breastfeeding families, an issue relevant for health equity. To our knowledge, no studies have assessed the direct financial costs associated with the purchase of commercially available breast pumps. In this cross-sectional study, we examined digital marketplaces in Germany for commercial electric breast pumps between March 2025 and May 2026, across major online platforms. Our objective was to explore pump features that predict price. We identified 282 commercial electric pump models from 108 brands. Basic information was unavailable for half of surveyed breast pump brands. The median price for surveyed commercial electric pumps was {euro}72.70 (IQR: {euro}82.70), with costs ranging widely from {euro}19.99 to {euro}659.57. Prices varied by marketplace, manufacturer location, accessories, pump system type, power source, battery capacity, flange sizes, availability of instruction manuals, and "single user" claims; predicting significantly higher costs. Half of pumps surveyed offered only one flange size, signaling additional expenses for mothers needing alternative sizes. These findings highlight important considerations for maternal health and consumer safety. Health technology assessments and a review of current health policy on reimbursement for commercial electric breast pumps is needed. Key messagesO_LITo our knowledge, there have been no published empirical studies on direct costs for commercial electric breast pumps C_LIO_LIBasic information was unavailable for half of the surveyed breast pump brands on digital marketplaces in Germany C_LIO_LIThe median cost for a commercial electric breast pump in our survey was {euro}72,70 (IQR: {euro}82,70), with a very wide price range ({euro}19,99 - {euro}659,57) C_LIO_LIPrices varied significantly by marketplace, manufacturer location, accessories, pump system type, power source, battery capacity, number of flange sizes, availability of instruction manuals, and "single user" claims, which all positively correlated with prices. C_LIO_LIThere is a sparsity of flange sizes sold outside of the mid-range (24 mm), signaling ancillary costs for flanges with appropriate fit C_LIO_LIHealth technology assessments for commercial electric breast pumps and a review of health policy related to breast pump reimbursement in Germany are warranted C_LI

papers.title: A multicountry trial-based and model-based economic evaluation of youth mental health interventions: a protocol for assessing the short- and long-term societal impacts of YOUTHreach interventions
authors: van Mastrigt, G. A. P. G.
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.12.26367972 v1

summary.background:
- Cost-effectiveness analysis compares the costs of an intervention with the health gains it produces, often expressed per unit of quality-adjusted life.
- Trial-based evaluation uses costs and outcomes collected alongside a randomised or controlled trial; model-based evaluation uses mathematical projections to estimate longer-term effects.
- "Care as usual" is the standard support people would receive without the new intervention.
- Societal perspective counts costs to the whole of society, not just the health budget, including lost productivity and unpaid care by family members.
- A resource use measurement instrument is a questionnaire used to record the services and time people use.
- A reference country is a chosen country whose prices and methods are used as the base case so that pooled multicountry results are consistent.
- Health technology assessment is the process bodies use to decide whether to fund a health intervention.
summary.one_liner: A study protocol describing harmonised trial-based and model-based economic evaluations of three youth mental health interventions (YEAH, SELFIE, MOST) against care as usual, with a shared multicountry resource-use measurement instrument.
summary.plain: This is a plan for measuring whether three programmes designed to help young people with mental health problems are good value for money, looking at costs well beyond the healthcare system, such as missed school, lost work, and unpaid family care. The researchers describe how they will follow participants for 12 months and then project costs and outcomes out to 10 years, using data pooled across several countries. The text is a protocol, so it reports no results.

papers.abstract: BackgroundMental health problems among young people impose a burden extending beyond healthcare, including impaired health-related quality of life and high societal costs from disrupted education, lost productivity, and informal care. Youth-friendly interventions may reduce this burden by providing early support and preventing escalation. However, their broader societal economic impact remains insufficiently explored. Evaluations incorporating consequences beyond healthcare and longer time horizons can better capture their societal value. MethodsThis protocol outlines harmonised trial-based and model-based economic evaluations of YEAH, SELFIE, and MOST, three mental health interventions for young people aged 12-25. Each intervention will be compared separately against care as usual over 12 months, with longer-term costs and outcomes projected at 2, 3, 5, and 10 years. Multicountry participant data will be pooled, using a prespecified reference country for base-case costing and methodological guidance. A harmonised, context-specific Resource Use Measurement instrument was developed to capture healthcare and broader societal resource use consistently across participating countries and to support evaluation of the economic impact of youth mental health interventions from a multicountry perspective. Uncertainty will be assessed through sensitivity and scenario analyses. DiscussionThe proposed harmonised methodological framework will support consistent estimation of the short- and long-term cost-effectiveness of three youth-friendly mental health interventions. It will enable comparison of intervention-specific results generated using different trial designs and support consistent estimation of costs and outcomes across the three interventions. The context-specific Resource Use Measurement instrument will further support consistent measurement of healthcare utilisation, productivity losses, and informal care across the economic evaluations. ConclusionBy integrating trial-based evidence with long-term modelling and standardised measurement of resource use, this study aims to generate robust, policy-relevant evidence to inform health technology assessment and decision-making for youth mental health interventions. The context-specific Resource Use Measurement instrument is also intended to support future economic evaluations of mental health interventions conducted across multiple countries.
